body_text: GCash is one of the most widely used payment methods in the Philippines with millions of users. If you sell anything, whether in a store, on social media, or through a website, some portion of your customers would rather pay with GCash than any other way. Accepting it is not complicated. But there are three distinct ways to do it, and they are not interchangeable. This guide explains each method, what it costs, and how to choose. The three ways to accept GCash Every business accepting GCash uses one of three mechanisms: Method How it works Best for Other payment methods QR Ph code Customer scans, pays from their wallet Counters, stalls, pop-ups, online checkouts Yes, QR Ph is wallet-agnostic GCash merchant account Direct relationship with GCash GCash-heavy physical retail No, GCash only Payment gateway GCash inside your checkout or payment links Online and social commerce Yes, cards, Maya, banks QR Ph codes generated through PayMongo can be paid with GCash, Maya, participating bank apps, and BNPL. The right choice depends on one question: where does the sale happen? If it happens at a counter, start with QR. If it happens in a chat thread or on a website, start with a link or gateway. Start Accepting GCash QR Ph: accepting GCash in person QR Ph is the national QR standard set by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. One property makes it useful: a single QR Ph code accepts payment from GCash, Maya, and most Philippine banking apps. The customer chooses the app; you display one code. There are two grades of QR. A personal QR, generated inside the GCash app, credits into your personal wallet. It works, but wallet limits apply and every payment mixes with your personal money. A business QR routes payments to a business account, with transaction records you can actually reconcile. You can obtain a business-grade QR Ph code either by applying to GCash directly, or instantly through PayMongo, where the same code also accepts Maya and bank app payments. Print the code. Place it where the customer already looks when it's time to pay. This is the entire integration. Get a QR Code Instantly The GCash merchant account GCash operates its own merchant program (GCash for Business). Applying gets you an official merchant QR, a business wallet, and GCash's merchant tooling. Three constraints are worth understanding before you apply. The account accepts GCash and nothing else, thus a customer holding a credit card or a Maya wallet cannot pay you through it. And it is built for in-person acceptance; selling online through it requires separate integration work. If your business is a physical store where most customers already pay with GCash, this is a reasonable choice. If any part of your selling happens online, it solves half the problem. Accepting GCash online Online, GCash acceptance runs through a payment gateway. Payment gateways usually provide two mechanisms, depending on whether you have a website. Payment links require no website; a social media page is enough. PayMongo asks for an active social media account at onboarding, and for most social sellers that's the Facebook or Instagram page they already sell from.You create a link, set the amount, and send it – Messenger, Viber, SMS, anywhere text goes. The customer opens it, pays with GCash (or a card, or Maya), and both sides receive confirmation. For businesses that close sales in conversations, the link goes where the conversation already is. Checkout integration puts GCash inside your website's payment flow. On Shopify and WooCommerce, this is a plug-in , not a development project. For custom-built sites, a payment API exposes the full payment flow – sessions, confirmations, webhooks. Setup, in either case: Create a PayMongo account. Free. No setup fee, no monthly fee. Verify your business. Business details and documents, submitted through the dashboard. Create a payment link, or install the plug-in. Both take minutes. Receive payouts. Funds settle to your bank account on a regular schedule. Sign Up What it costs Pricing is usually the deciding factor, so here is the honest comparison of a GCash merchant account and a payment gateway like PayMongo: Method Transaction fee Personal GCash QR Free, within wallet limits GCash merchant account 1% (QR Ph), 3.2% (Mastercard/Visa) PayMongo (GCash) 1.34% (QR Ph - accepts various payment methods), 3.125% (Mastercard/Visa) PayMongo charges only on successful transactions; no setup fee, no monthly fee. Making it visible Accepting GCash only converts sales if customers know before they hesitate. State it where purchase decisions happen: store signage, your Facebook page, product listings, your checkout page. If you sell through DMs, send the payment link inside the same conversation – every app-switch or typed account number is a place where a sale quietly dies. Additionally, keep the alternatives on. Some customers will always prefer Maya, a card, or a bank transfer. Accepting all of them through one account means the payment method is never the reason you lose the sale. Start Accepting GCash: Your customers already have GCash on their phones. PayMongo puts it in your checkout, alongside cards, Maya, QR Ph, and online banking, with no setup fees and nothing to build. Create a free account Frequently Asked Questions Can I accept GCash payments without a business account? Yes. A personal GCash wallet accepts payments by QR or send-money. Wallet limits apply, and payments mix with personal funds. For registered businesses, a merchant account or gateway provides higher limits, receipts, and clean records. How do I get a GCash QR code for my business? Two routes: apply through GCash for Business, or generate a QR Ph code through PayMongo. The PayMongo code also accepts Maya and participating bank apps. Do I need DTI or SEC registration? Not for a personal wallet. For a GCash merchant account or a PayMongo business account: DTI registration for sole proprietors, SEC for corporations. Freelancers can apply to PayMongo as individuals. Read more: What Is QRPH? Everything Filipino Merchants Need to Know How to Accept Payments Online? title: 11 Free Job Boards for Employers in 2026
summary: Compare 11 free job boards for high-volume frontline hiring in 2026, plus the agentic hiring system that turns free applicant flow into actual hires.
body_text: Free job boards still have a place in frontline hiring, but comparing boards alone misses the 2026 shift. Software is becoming the back end of hiring, and agents are becoming the front end that screens applicants, schedules interviews, answers questions, and keeps onboarding moving. Free posting reach and organic visibility on the biggest boards have grown less predictable over time, so a free-only strategy built on a single board no longer holds for employers filling hundreds of roles across dozens of locations. This guide covers both: the 11 best free boards for applicant flow, and the hiring system that converts that flow into hires. Applicant volume now depends less on the posting site and more on the workflow that responds before candidates accept another offer. Fountain’s Redefining Frontline Operations research finds that many applicants abandon applications that feel too long or aren’t mobile-optimized, and the best hourly candidates often accept the first offer they get within a day or two. Free reach gets you applicants. What you do next decides whether you hire them. What free job boards do (and don’t) for frontline hiring A free job board publishes your opening at no cost and sometimes syndicates it to other sites. It supplies applicant flow, but it does not screen, schedule, or follow up, and in frontline hiring that gap is where roles are won or lost. High-volume employers pair free reach with a hiring system that converts it. Fountain: The frontline hiring and workforce management platform, purpose-built for high-volume hiring with agentic screening, scheduling, and onboarding while your team makes the final call. Google for Jobs: Broad free reach that surfaces career-site listings in search results. Facebook Jobs: A supplemental channel to test for local, shift-based, hourly roles. Indeed: High traffic, but free posting and organic reach have grown less predictable, so it works best as one channel among several. Craigslist: Free or low-cost hyper-local posting for retail, warehouse, and service roles. PostJobFree: A free posting channel that extends distribution to other job sites. SimplyHired: A wide-reach aggregator with free posting for general distribution. Handshake: A large early-career network for campus and entry-level hiring. LinkedIn Jobs: A limited free option, better for professional roles than frontline volume. Learn4Good: A limited free option for early-career hourly seekers. iCIMS: Enterprise ATS with a Frontline AI layer, strongest for organizations already on iCIMS. The sections below rank both the boards and the hiring systems for one job: filling frontline roles at high volume without burning your budget or your recruiters. How to evaluate a free job board for frontline hiring A free board helps only if your team can screen, schedule, and reply before applicants take another offer. Most frontline talent acquisition (TA) teams over-index on reach and under-index on what happens after the click. Mobile-first reach: Most frontline candidates apply from their phones, often between shifts, so a board that drives mobile traffic into a desktop-first form wastes the reach. Frontline and hourly fit: General aggregators reach everyone, while boards built for hourly and shift-based roles reach the people who actually fill cashier, driver, and warehouse positions. Posting volume and syndication: Free tiers with hard caps may not support hiring across 200 locations, and boards that push your listing to other channels multiply free reach without multiplying work. Screening and automation: Most free boards stop at posting and distribution, so check whether your hiring system can screen, schedule, and message candidates once that volume arrives. Free boards deliver reach. The hiring system that follows handles what reach alone cannot: converting applicants into hires fast enough to win. Platform Type Named agent/product layer Best role in a frontline hiring mix Fountain Frontline hiring platform Cue orchestrator plus Anna, Emma, Sam; ATS, Sourcing, CRM, Onboarding, Shift & Scheduling High-volume hourly hiring, screening to Day 1 Google for Jobs Search aggregator None Broad search visibility from a structured career site Facebook Jobs Social channel None Local, shift-based, and hourly role testing Indeed Job board None in the free layer High-traffic sourcing for entry-level and hourly roles Craigslist Classifieds None Hyper-local retail, warehouse, and service hiring PostJobFree Posting plus syndication None Free syndication volume across additional sites SimplyHired Aggregator None General aggregator reach for multi-channel sourcing Handshake Early-career network None Campus, student, and early-career hiring LinkedIn Jobs Professional network None in the free tier Occasional professional or specialized roles Learn4Good Job board None Early-career and hourly seekers, manual handling iCIMS Enterprise ATS Frontline AI suite Enterprises already standardized on iCIMS The profiles below explain why each earned its row. What are the best free job boards and platforms for frontline hiring? 1. Fountain Fountain is the frontline hiring and workforce management platform purpose-built for high-volume hourly hiring, hiring 1.2 million workers annually across quick-service restaurants (QSR), retail, logistics, and outsourced services. The hardest part of frontline hiring starts after the application arrives, and that is where Fountain runs agentic screening, self-scheduling, onboarding, and compliance while managers approve every hire. Proof points: START BUILDING SMARTER—NOT JUST FASTER Download the Free Guide: How Agentic AI Is Transforming Frontline Hiring Discover how today’s most innovative HR teams are rethinking hiring, onboarding, and retention—from fragmented tasks to coordinated, goal-driven systems. No more manual handoffs. No guesswork. Just intelligent automation that adapts and delivers. If you’re managing high-volume roles and want to stay ahead of rising talent demands, this guide is your blueprint. Download the White Paper Bojangles , a 750-location QSR chain, cut time-to-hire from 30 days to 5.8 days (an 80% reduction) and dropped job-board spend by 86%. Fetch grew applicant volume 325% to 10,000 a month and reduced time-to-hire 95%, from 15 days to 6.5 hours, with AI voice screening. Liveops , a virtual contact center, cut time-to-fill by 48% while a nine-person recruiting team scaled to roughly 400,000 applications a year. Best for: High-volume frontline employers in QSR, retail, logistics, and outsourced services filling hundreds of roles across many locations. Fit caveat: Not the right fit for salaried corporate hiring or a one-off free posting; Fountain is a hiring platform, not a standalone posting site. 2. Google for Jobs Google for Jobs aggregates listings from employer career sites into search results, offering broad free reach with no posting interface: you mark up career-site jobs with structured data, and Google surfaces them. Visibility depends on Google’s ranking, and there is no built-in screening or scheduling, so it works best paired with an ATS that handles the applicant flow it sends. Best for: Frontline employers with a structured career site who want maximum free reach. 3. Facebook Jobs Facebook can be a practical channel to test for local, shift-based roles where candidates live near the location and use the platform daily. Reach varies by market, and you will need to manage screening, tracking, and follow-up in your own hiring system. Best for: QSR, retail, and service employers hiring hourly workers for specific locations. 4. Indeed Indeed remains a high-traffic job site, but its free value for high-volume employers has become less predictable as free posting rules and organic reach on large boards have shifted over time. It still reaches hourly candidates at scale, but its free limits make it a supplementary channel rather than a foundation. Best for: Employers filling a few roles at a time, or high-volume teams willing to fund sponsored posts. 5. Craigslist Craigslist is still a practical option for hyper-local, budget-friendly hiring in retail, warehouse, and service roles where candidates live nearby. There are no screening or tracking features, so everything after the posting is on your team. Best for: Small to mid-size employers hiring hourly workers in a specific area who can manage applicants manually. 6. PostJobFree PostJobFree is a free posting option that can syndicate your listing to other job sites, so its value is in reach and distribution rather than candidate management. It carries no built-in screening, so pair it with a system that handles screening and tracking. Best for: Cost-conscious employers adding free syndication volume to their sourcing mix. 7. SimplyHired SimplyHired is a wide-reach aggregator with free posting options that distribute listings broadly. It is a solid supplementary channel, though general-purpose rather than frontline-specific, with no built-in screening. Best for: Employers building a multi-channel free sourcing strategy beyond Indeed and Google for Jobs. 8. Handshake Handshake is a major early-career network partnering directly with universities, useful for reaching younger and campus-adjacent talent. Response rates on broad, unfocused applications tend to run low, so treat it as a targeted channel for campus and entry-level hiring rather than the core source for urgent shift coverage. Best for: Retail and QSR chains recruiting younger workers and campus-adjacent entry-level roles. 9. LinkedIn Jobs For frontline hiring, LinkedIn Jobs suits occasional professional or specialized roles more than hourly volume, and the free tier’s limits make it a low-priority channel for shift-based hiring at scale. Best for: Employers hiring professional or specialized roles alongside their frontline pipeline. 10. Learn4Good Learn4Good is a limited free posting option with modest reach, best for hiring students or early-career hourly seekers in education, healthcare, or service roles. It has no built-in screening and handles applications manually, so confirm current posting terms first. Best for: Smaller employers recruiting students and early-career candidates who can handle applications by hand. 11. iCIMS iCIMS is an enterprise ATS that, in Spring 2026, launched iCIMS Frontline AI , a candidate-engagement layer across SMS, WhatsApp, and web built on its Apli acquisition. For existing iCIMS enterprises, that can close mobile-channel response gaps after candidates apply, but teams buying only for frontline hiring may get more enterprise setup than they need. Best for: Large enterprises already running iCIMS for corporate recruiting who want frontline hiring on the same platform. How Fountain turns free-board applicant flow into hires Free boards drive volume; Fountain converts it. Fountain delivers Frontline Superintelligence, a coordinated agentic execution layer for the frontline workforce. At the top sits Cue , which takes plain-English hiring goals like “hire 10 drivers before Monday” and routes work across sourcing, screening, onboarding, and scheduling, flagging where candidates stall and triggering the next step. Under Cue sit three named agents. Anna conducts real voice interviews 24/7, scores candidates, and pushes qualified applicants to managers, with a human making the final hiring call. Fountain’s 2025 Fountain Frontline Report finds that most frontline workers now prefer AI voice interviews to waiting for a scheduled call. Emma walks new hires through I-9, W-4, and onboarding paperwork over SMS, voice, and web chat. Sam runs Day 1, Day 10, and Day 30 pulse checks to catch retention risks before workers quit. The agents operate on a mobile-first ATS , Onboarding with E-Verify and document processing, native Shift & Scheduling , a CRM that re-activates past applicants, and native integrations with UKG, SAP, ADP, and Workday. The friction the free boards leave behind, thousands of applicants and no fast way to screen them, is what agents running the operational work resolve. If your operation is ready to turn free-board volume into filled shifts, book a demo to watch Cue translate a hiring goal into coordinated tasks, Anna screen real candidates by voice, and Sam catch retention risks before Day 30. Frequently asked questions about free job boards for frontline hiring What is the best free job board for high-volume hourly hiring? For free reach, Google for Jobs offers broad distribution when paired with a structured career site, and Facebook Jobs is worth testing for local shift-based roles. Indeed still reaches hourly candidates at scale, but its free posting limits reduce its usefulness for high-volume employers. No single free board handles high-volume hiring end to end, since they stop at the posting and leave screening and scheduling to your team. Why do free job boards fall short for frontline hiring at scale? Free boards drive applicant volume, but conversion depends on what happens after the application starts. Many applicants abandon applications that feel too long or aren’t mobile-optimized, and the best hourly candidates often accept the first offer they get within a day or two. Without a fast process for screening, scheduling, and communication, that volume lands on recruiters who cannot move fast enough at high volume to beat competitors to the offer. Should I use a free job board or a frontline hiring platform? Use both. Free boards like Google for Jobs, Facebook Jobs, and PostJobFree feed the top of your funnel at no cost, and Fountain’s roundup of free candidate sourcing tools covers the no-cost ground for the smallest operations. A frontline hiring platform then handles what reach cannot: screening thousands of applicants, scheduling interviews, and moving them to Day 1 fast. For occasional low-volume hiring, free boards alone may suffice; for high-volume hiring across many locations, you need a platform to convert that reach into hires.

title: Single-Center vs Multi-Center Studies: What We've Learned About Scaling Imaging AI
summary: Explore how single-center vs multi-center imaging studies impact AI generalizability, validation, and scalable real-world deployment.
body_text: ‍ From Proof-of-Concept to Scale ‍ Over the past ten years, artificial intelligence (AI) has progressed from research-oriented prototypes to clinical decision support systems in medical imaging. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved more than a thousand AI/ML-assisted medical devices , the majority of which are imaging-based. The early successes of imaging AI often begin in the highly resourceful academic setting. A research team, often affiliated with a leading technical university, collaborates with a renowned academic medical center. The purpose of this collaboration is to leverage a carefully curated retrospective dataset precisely matching the target application of the AI model. These datasets usually have structured reporting, uniform imaging protocols, stable scanner configurations, and relatively complete metadata. In such controlled settings, model development is rapid as datasets are easily standardized and clinical outcomes are well-defined. Internal validation of such AI models demonstrates excellent performance characteristics such as high area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity because the training and validation datasets share a common institutional fingerprint. However, this success may be more a result of intra-institutional optimization than true generalizability. When the same model is deployed in the real world, several destabilizing factors emerge. These include variability in data structure and demographics, imaging acquisition heterogeneity, workflow artifacts and other hidden confounders.1,2 ‍ Defining Single-Center vs Multi-Center Imaging Studies ‍ A single-center study derives all data from one institution, often a single academic hospital or health system. Data typically share common characteristics such as uniform scanner fleet (e.g., limited vendors/models), standardized acquisition protocols, consistent reporting language, homogeneous patient referral patterns. Such datasets offer low variance and tight control over confounders. While, a multi-center study aggregates data across two or more independent institutions. These institutions may differ in geography and patient demographics, scanner vendors and software versions. They may also vary in imaging protocols, clinical documentation practices and care delivery settings including academic, community, specialty hospitals. ‍ The degree of heterogeneity between both kinds of studies varies substantially. The table above represents the heterogeneity in key structural elements of both of the studies. ‍ ‍ The Promise and Pitfalls of Single-Center Studies ‍ Single-center datasets have been the backbone of modern imaging AI development. For early innovation and feasibility studies and proof-of-concept models, such conditions are not only convenient but they are strategically appropriate. Apart from standardization in data collection and storage, single-center studies offer advantages such as tight collaboration between clinicians and data scientists. From a modeling perspective, single-center AI model development reduces unwanted variance and allows algorithms to identify clinically relevant signals with greater statistical efficiency. Feedback loops between model developers and clinical stakeholders are proactive. Iterative refinements adjusting labeling strategies, recalibrating thresholds, or testing architectural changes can occur without the logistical burden of cross-site coordination. If a tool is intended for deployment within the same institutional ecosystem in which it was trained, performance may likely remain stable. ‍ “Single-center datasets accelerate innovation, but they can also encode institutional fingerprints into AI models.” ‍ The difficulty arises when institutional optimization is mistaken for generalizability. Evidence from cross-hospital evaluations suggests that models trained in homogeneous environments often encode site-specific characteristics rather than purely pathological features. Research published in NPJ Digital Medicine showed that deep learning systems could leverage hospital process artifacts, rather than disease biology to generate predictions. These findings highlight a structural vulnerability: models may internalize contextual signals such as scanner-specific noise patterns, acquisition conventions, or workflow correlates that do not transfer beyond the originating site. ‍ Demographic and technical homogeneity compound the issue. A single institution reflects a specific referral base, socioeconomic distribution, and disease prevalence profile. Scanner vendors, hardware generations, and reconstruction techniques may be limited in such scenarios. Without exposure to broader variability during training, models risk uneven performance across patient subgroups. Disparities in algorithmic performance across race and sex have been documented in imaging AI systems. One such example includes an analysis published in Nature Medicine , underscoring the importance of representative data during development. ‍ Perhaps the most persistent risk is misplaced confidence derived from internal validation. When training and test sets are sampled from the same institution. Many imaging AI studies lack rigorous external validation and may therefore overestimate real-world readiness. Across multiple evaluations, measurable declines in performance have been observed when models are assessed outside their training institution. In practical terms, a model that achieves 0.95 AUC internally may experience meaningful degradation once exposed to new patient populations, scanner ecosystems, and documentation practices. Single-center studies remain essential for innovation, but without external validation, they measure optimization not scalability. Why Multi-Center Data Changes Everything? ‍ “Multi-center datasets stress-tests AI systems before they reach clinical environments.” ‍ Multi-center data fundamentally reshape how imaging AI systems are trained and evaluated because they introduce structured exposure to real-world heterogeneity. Differences in patient populations, care settings across institutions cause variability in imaging data. Scanner vendors, software versions, field strengths, and reconstruction pipelines are all examples of how images vary due to technical characteristics of different imaging systems. Variability exists even if two centers are using the same scanner model; different acquisition parameters and reconstruction methods can be found due to local protocols or different preferences of radiologists at each center. These seemingly minor discrepancies result in images that have different characteristics than anticipated and can create measurement shifts that aren't apparent during single-center development. By using multi-center images for training, pathological features that occur consistently across the sites are learned by the cross-site model, rather than by training on site-specific characteristics alone. These advantages lead to improvements in generalizability and stability. Studies involving more than one institution have provided ample evidence that there is usually a decrease in how well models work when they are tested at different institutions from where they were developed. Declines in model performance when utilized in different settings are often not indicative of a flaw in the model; rather, they are commonly attributable to the distribution shifts a model encounters when being used outside its normal site of development. Through the use of multi-center validation, potential weaknesses are identified early and offer opportunities for recalibrating models prior to implementation in the clinical setting. Broader datasets allow stratified evaluation across demographic groups and care environments, helping to uncover hidden biases that single-center cohorts may obscure. External validation across independent institutions has therefore become central to clinical trust and regulatory confidence.3,4 ‍ Lessons Learned from Real-World Imaging Data at Scale ‍ Working with globally distributed imaging datasets makes one principle unmistakably clear: heterogeneity is the norm, not the exception. Across institutions and geographies, variability appears in metadata completeness, reporting language, labeling standards, and annotation consistency. Even when imaging pixels appear comparable, the surrounding clinical context often differs. Effective harmonization therefore requires more than technical normalization; it demands clinical insight to distinguish meaningful variation from noise. This variability creates a natural tension between data complexity and model readiness. Highly heterogeneous datasets introduce statistical noise, may slow early convergence, and often require larger sample sizes or domain adaptation techniques. However, models trained under such conditions tend to be more resilient at deployment. Exposure to diverse scanners, protocols, and patient populations during development reduces reliance on site-specific artifacts and improves robustness under distribution shift. At scale, it also becomes clear that data strategy must evolve alongside algorithm maturity. Early AI efforts often emphasize dataset volume to establish innovation feasibility. Over time, representativeness becomes more critical than size alone. A structured progression typically strengthens generalizability. In an award-winning study performed by the Segmed team , radiology reporting patterns were examined for oligometastatic disease. Specialty oncology centers demonstrated higher adoption of the term compared with general hospitals. A single cancer-center study would therefore overestimate prevalence relative to a broader multi-center sample. This underscores a broader reality, institutional culture influences not only imaging acquisition but also diagnostic terminology. AI systems incorporating NLP or structured reporting signals must explicitly account for such heterogeneity to avoid embedding linguistic bias into model outputs. ‍ Conclusion: Data as the Foundation for Scalable Imaging AI ‍ Single-center studies remain indispensable to the advancement of imaging AI . They provide the controlled conditions necessary for hypothesis testing, rapid iteration, foundation model and early performance validation. Yet scalability demands a different benchmark. Multi-center validation is the mechanism through which these become attainable. It reveals whether a model is resilient to distributional changes and whether performance holds across institutions that differ in geography, patient mix, technical infrastructure, and reporting culture. Without such validation, strong internal metrics risk overstating clinical readiness. As imaging AI matures, the methodological expectation is becoming clearer. Internal validation demonstrates feasibility within a defined environment. External, multi-center validation demonstrates durability across environments. Ultimately, scalable imaging AI is not achieved through algorithmic sophistication alone. Model architecture, training strategies, and computational efficiency matter but they cannot compensate for diverse and unrepresentative data. Robustness emerges from deliberate exposure to real-world heterogeneity during development and validation. ‍ Multi-Center Validation with Segmed: The Path to Scalable AI ‍ With the transition from development to implementation of imaging AI, the capability to validate across various clinical contexts is key. While it may be possible to achieve excellent results using training data sets from a single-center, the real test of scalability is the generalizability across centers, demographics, and imaging modalities. By leveraging our extensive network of partners, Segmed allows access to large, multi-center imaging data sets, which simulate real-life diversity. By virtue of wide geographical representation and diversified imaging contexts, our data sets can facilitate external validation, bias evaluation, and performance benchmarking of AI models. ‍ Get in touch to learn more about how multi-center imaging data can help you develop AI models that are accurate, robust, and ready for real-world clinical use. ‍ ‍ Frequented Asked Questions - F.A.Q. What is the difference between single-center and multi-center imaging studies? The difference between single-center and multi-center imaging studies lies in the number of institutions contributing imaging data and how that affects data variability, generalizability, and model robustness. A single-center study collects imaging data from one hospital or institution. Key characteristics: Uniform scanner vendors and protocols Homogeneous patient population Consistent acquisition parameters Limited demographic diversity Advantages: Controlled environment Faster execution Lower operational complexity Limitations: High risk of overfitting Limited external validity Poor generalizability to other healthcare settings A multi-center study aggregates imaging data from multiple hospitals or research institutions. Key characteristics: Diverse scanner manufacturers Variable acquisition protocols Broader demographic representation Greater real-world variability Advantages: Improved model robustness Better generalizability Reduced institutional bias Higher regulatory credibility Limitations: Increased logistical complexity Data harmonization challenges Regulatory and data-sharing barriers Bottom Line Single-center datasets often fail to capture real-world heterogeneity in clinical imaging. Multi-center imaging studies better reflect real-world deployment conditions and are considered the gold standard for validating AI models in radiology and medical imaging. ‍ Why do AI models perform worse during external validation? AI models frequently show performance degradation during external validation because they encounter data distributions that differ from the training dataset. This phenomenon is primarily driven by distribution shifts. Key causes of performance drop include: Domain Shift- Differences in scanner vendors, imaging protocols, reconstruction algorithms. Even subtle technical differences can significantly alter pixel intensity distributions. Demographic Variation- Training data may underrepresent: ethnic minorities, pediatric or geriatric populations, rare disease subtypes, etc. Models trained on narrow populations fail when applied to broader groups. Overfitting to Institutional Artifacts- Models may inadvertently learn site-specific metadata, scanner-specific noise patterns, institutional annotation styles. These features do not generalize externally. ‍ Why is multi-center validation important in medical imaging AI? Multi-center validation is critical for ensuring robustness, fairness, and regulatory readiness of AI models in medical imaging. Exposure to heterogeneous datasets allows models to learn invariant features, reduce overfitting, and perform reliably across institutions and reflects real-world implementation. Multi-center validation also boosts clinical and regulatory credibility. Regulatory agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency expect evidence of performance across diverse populations before approving AI-based medical devices. ‍ How does dataset bias affect imaging AI performance? Dataset bias occurs when training data does not accurately represent the target population or real-world variability. This significantly impacts imaging AI performance. Consequences of Dataset Bias: Reduced external validation performance Increased false positives/negatives Amplification of healthcare disparities Regulatory rejection Loss of clinician trust Mitigation Strategies: Multi-center data aggregation Data harmonization techniques Prospective external validation Federated learning approaches ‍ References Kelly CJ, Karthikesalingam A, Suleyman M, Corrado G, King D. title: Tariff Volatility Is the New Normal: Here’s How Supply Chain Leaders Are Adapting
summary: Tariff volatility isn’t temporary. Learn why the real competitive edge is execution speed, not forecasting, and how leading suppliers are adapting.
body_text: In this article, learn about: Why treating “wait and see” as a safe, neutral posture is itself a growing risk What the data shows about how supply chain leaders are reprioritizing around tariff volatility What the “musical factories” pattern looks like across three real supplier moves How closing the gap between a sourcing decision and its execution, the exact problem SPS Fulfillment is built to solve, determines who adapts fastest Tariff rates have eased off their 2025 peaks, and for a lot of supply chain leaders, that’s started to feel like an opening to exhale. It isn’t one. The instinct right now is to pause sourcing decisions and wait for policy to settle before committing to anything structural. This makes sense on the surface. It’s also the wrong read on where things stand. Certainty isn’t coming back. Tariff volatility has stopped being a periodic disruption and started being the standing condition suppliers operate under, which means “wait and see” isn’t a neutral holding pattern. It’s a slow bleed of optionality, since every quarter spent waiting is a quarter competitors spend closing the gap between deciding to move and actually moving. The suppliers pulling ahead aren't the ones who've guessed tariff policy correctly so much as they have cut enough friction out of that gap, so a pivot takes weeks instead of quarters. Why Is “Wait and See” the Riskier Move Right Now? The moment can look like relief from the outside. The people closest to the problem aren’t reading it that way. The Thomson Reuters 2026 Global Trade Report found that 72 percent of trade professionals now name U.S. tariff volatility as the single most impactful regulatory change they face, up from 41 percent a year earlier. Supply chain management has climbed to the top strategic priority for 68 percent of respondents, nearly double the 35 percent who said the same the year before. The C-suite is telling a similar story. Seventy-one percent of U.S. CEOs now plan to alter their supply chains over the next three to five years, up sharply from 54 percent in last year’s survey. Those numbers don’t read like people expecting the volatility to fade. The calm stretch is a window to build adaptive capacity, not a rest stop. Waiting it out doesn’t pause the risk, but it hands the advantage to whoever spent the same months getting faster. Related Reading: Staying Agile in the Face of Tariffs How Are Leading Suppliers Approaching Sourcing Diversification? The resilience advice hasn’t changed much: diversify suppliers , keep visibility on inventory, move faster on onboarding. What’s changed is how urgently suppliers are actually following it. McKinsey’s geopolitics research centers on assessing and diversifying supplier networks and keeping production flexible enough to shift product flows when disruptions hit. The more useful nuance sits in McKinsey’s own supply chain risk survey : tariffs have mostly accelerated resilience strategies suppliers were already pursuing, rather than sending them in a new direction. The priority is speed on approaches that already work. Nobody credible is calling for a ground-up rebuild. That acceleration matters more given how little most suppliers can see past their own front door. Only 42 percent of global supply chain executives say they understand the operations of suppliers below their first tier, a smaller share than in 2022. Layer in how concentrated some categories still are overseas, only about 1 percent of toys and 3 percent of fashion goods get made domestically, and leaving the region simply isn’t on the table for most suppliers in these categories. Diversification and visibility are the baseline for staying in the game. Treating them as a someday upgrade is how a supplier gets caught flat. What Does the “Musical Factories” Pattern Look Like? Diversifying suppliers is easy to say and hard to execute, since the volatility doesn’t stop once a supplier moves, and it doesn’t move in one direction. Steve Madden is the clearest example of what that back-and-forth costs. The footwear and accessories company cut its China sourcing sharply through 2025, then moved some fall 2025 production back once it was clear alternative countries couldn’t match China on delivery, quality, or price. Fall 2025 sourcing from China landed around 30 percent, down from 71 percent in 2024. What made the reversal possible was a supplier base flexible enough to move back without starting over. Not every supplier is solving the same version of this problem. Lindt & Sprüngli shows the contrast. Instead of rebuilding a sourcing base under pressure, the confectionery maker rerouted chocolate production from its U.S. factories to Europe to fill Canadian orders and sidestep retaliatory tariffs, using a distributed footprint it already had in place. In consumer electronics, HP expanded sourcing to Taiwan and Thailand after tariffs hit its China-based supply, cutting costs by roughly 8 percent, while acknowledging that the added complexity called for stronger supplier-management systems to run it. Company Category Adaptation move Infrastructure it required Steve Madden Apparel and footwear Cut China sourcing to about 30 percent for fall 2025, then reversed part of it when alternatives fell short on delivery and quality A supplier base flexible enough to move back within a season Lindt & Sprüngli Food and confectionery Rerouted chocolate production from U.S. factories to Europe to fill Canadian orders A distributed footprint that could redirect volume without rebuilding it HP Consumer electronics Expanded sourcing to Taiwan and Thailand, cutting costs by about 8 percent Supplier-management systems built for a more complex network The pivot is only as good as the infrastructure underneath it. Diversifying suppliers doesn’t help much if reconnecting data with a new manufacturing partner still takes months, and it doesn’t help at all if a supplier can’t move back once the numbers change again. Why Is the Real Bottleneck Execution, Not Strategy? Here’s what most resilience advice skips: these moves aren’t free, and the cost usually isn’t the sourcing decision itself. Leadership can change sourcing strategy in a single meeting. Everything downstream of that decision takes months instead, like onboarding a new factory partner , re-mapping inventory and item data, and reconnecting order and shipment data across every retailer and distributor a supplier sells into. That gap is what actually determines whether a strategy survives contact with the next tariff shift. A sourcing decision that takes weeks to execute is a real advantage. The same decision stranded behind months of manual onboarding and disconnected systems arrives too late to matter, no matter how sound it looked on the board slide. A connected supplier network changes that math. When onboarding a new factory partner, or reconnecting item, order, and shipment data, doesn’t mean rebuilding the technical relationship from scratch each time, because the network has already handled similar onboarding hundreds of times before, the decision-to-execution gap shrinks from months to weeks. SPS Fulfillment is built around exactly that problem: getting a new supplier relationship live in weeks instead of months, so a sourcing decision doesn’t sit stranded while the systems catch up. Related Reading: Tariff Refunds: The Operational Nightmare Businesses Aren’t Ready For Why Is the Calm Stretch the Build Window? Go back to the “moment of relief” framing. Tariff rates easing doesn’t mean the volatility is over, and the professionals closest to the problem don’t expect a return to stability either: most respondents in the Thomson Reuters report expect continued disruption over the next six to twelve months. That’s exactly why this stretch matters. A calm quarter spent waiting is a calm quarter a competitor spent compressing their reaction time. The suppliers who use it that way, closing the distance between a sourcing decision and its execution, won’t be scrambling when conditions shift again. The ones who spent it waiting will be. Frequently Asked Questions Is tariff volatility a temporary situation or a lasting shift? The data points toward lasting. Trade professionals in the Thomson Reuters 2026 Global Trade Report expect continued disruption over the next six to twelve months, and supply chain management has become a top strategic priority for a majority of respondents rather than a passing concern. What should supply chain leaders prioritize right now? Supplier diversification and inventory visibility still matter, but the research points to a bigger lever: shortening the time between a sourcing decision and its execution across onboarding, inventory, and order data. Why does execution speed matter more than predicting tariff policy? Tariff policy has proven difficult to predict, and the suppliers adapting best haven’t been the ones who guessed correctly. They’ve been the ones who could act on a decision in weeks rather than months, regardless of which way policy moved next. What does the “musical factories” pattern mean? It describes suppliers moving production in response to tariffs, then moving it again, sometimes back to where they started, as conditions shift. Steve Madden’s move out of China and partial return is the clearest recent example. Want to Close the Gap Between a Sourcing Decision and Its Execution? The suppliers moving fastest right now aren’t the ones with the best tariff forecast. They’re the ones who built a supplier network that keeps sourcing decisions and their execution close together instead of months apart. SPS Fulfillment helps new supplier and retailer relationships go live in weeks, not months, so the next sourcing decision doesn’t get stranded behind onboarding and reconnection work. title: 7 Ultra-Processed Food Ingredients to Limit for Better Long-Term Health

body_text: Ultr- processed foods have become a staple in many households because they are affordable, convenient, and widely available. From breakfast cereals and packaged snacks to ready meals and soft drinks, these products save time and often satisfy cravings. However, growing research suggests that regularly eating large amounts of ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of several chronic health conditions. The issue is not that every processed food is unhealthy. Many foods undergo some level of processing to improve safety or shelf life. The concern is with ultra-processed foods , which often contain multiple additives, refined ingredients, added sugars, unhealthy fats, and preservatives designed to improve flavor, texture, and appearance. Instead of avoiding these foods entirely, understanding which ingredients deserve extra attention can help you make smarter choices. Here are seven ingredients commonly found in ultra-processed foods that experts recommend limiting. 1. Artificial Food Colorings Artificial food colorings are synthetic dyes added to make foods look more attractive. They are commonly found in candies, flavored drinks, breakfast cereals, desserts, and packaged snacks. Some research has linked certain artificial colors to behavioral changes in children, including increased hyperactivity and attention difficulties in susceptible individuals. Because of these concerns, some countries require warning labels or encourage manufacturers to reduce their use. Rather than relying on brightly colored processed snacks, choose foods colored naturally with fruits, vegetables, or spices whenever possible. 2. Nitrates and Nitrites in Processed Meats Processed meats such as bacon, sausages, hot dogs, ham, and deli meats often contain nitrates and nitrites. These preservatives help maintain color, extend shelf life, and prevent bacterial growth. Scientists are concerned because nitrites can form compounds called nitrosamines under certain conditions. These compounds have been associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer. This does not mean you need to eliminate processed meat forever. Instead, treat these foods as occasional choices rather than everyday staples. Replacing some servings with fresh poultry, fish, beans, or lean cuts of meat may help reduce overall exposure. 3. Certain Emulsifiers Emulsifiers are additives that help ingredients like oil and water mix together. They improve texture and prevent foods from separating during storage. Common emulsifiers appear in products such as: Packaged bread Ice cream Ready meals Salad dressings Frozen desserts Processed sauces Some studies suggest that specific emulsifiers may alter the gut microbiome and contribute to inflammation. While research is still ongoing, reducing heavily processed foods naturally lowers your intake of these additives. 4. High Fructose Corn Syrup High fructose corn syrup is a sweetener widely used in soft drinks, packaged desserts, candies, sauces, and many processed foods. Unlike naturally occurring sugars found in whole fruit, this ingredient is often consumed in large quantities through sweetened beverages and snacks. Excessive intake has been linked with obesity, insulin resistance, fatty liver disease, and type 2 diabetes. One of the easiest ways to reduce intake is by replacing sugary beverages with water, sparkling water, or unsweetened tea. 5. Refined Added Sugars Not all added sugar comes from high fructose corn syrup. Manufacturers use many different names, including cane sugar, glucose syrup, corn syrup, malt syrup, and invert sugar. Consuming excessive added sugar contributes to: Weight gain Tooth decay Increased risk of type 2 diabetes Higher risk of cardiovascular disease Reading ingredient labels can help you identify products that contain multiple added sweeteners. 6. Excess Sodium Salt plays an important role in preserving packaged foods and enhancing flavor. Unfortunately, many ready meals, canned soups, frozen dinners, instant noodles, and savory snacks contain far more sodium than most people realize. High sodium intake has been linked to elevated blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart disease and stroke. Cooking more meals at home and choosing lower sodium versions of packaged foods can significantly reduce daily intake. 7. Highly Refined Vegetable Oils and Engineered Fats Many packaged baked goods, pastries, cookies, spreads, and snack foods contain refined vegetable oils or specially modified fats that improve texture and shelf life. Although these fats replaced industrial trans fats in many products, researchers continue studying their long term health effects. Since these ingredients are most common in heavily processed foods, eating more minimally processed meals naturally reduces exposure. Why Ingredient Lists Matter One simple habit can improve your grocery shopping decisions: read the ingredient list before buying packaged foods. A shorter ingredient list with recognizable foods often indicates less processing. Products containing numerous additives, preservatives, artificial colors, flavor enhancers, and stabilizers are generally more processed. Nutrition labels also provide valuable information about added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat, allowing you to compare similar products. You Do Not Need to Avoid Every Processed Food It is important to remember that processing exists on a spectrum. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, plain yogurt, whole-grain bread, and pasteurized milk are processed foods, yet they can still be nutritious choices. The greatest concern comes from diets where ultra-processed foods make up the majority of daily calories. Occasional treats are unlikely to have a major impact when balanced with an overall healthy eating pattern. Simple Ways to Reduce Ultra-Processed Foods Making small, realistic changes is often more sustainable than attempting a complete diet overhaul. Consider these practical strategies: Eat more fresh fruits and vegetables. Choose whole grains when possible. Cook simple meals at home several times each week. Replace sugary drinks with water. Snack on nuts, fruit, or yogurt instead of packaged sweets. Compare ingredient labels before purchasing. Limit processed meats to occasional meals. Small improvements made consistently over time can support better overall health without making eating feel restrictive. Final Thoughts Ultra-processed foods are unlikely to disappear from modern diets, and they can still have a place in a balanced lifestyle. However, paying closer attention to ingredients such as artificial colors, nitrites, emulsifiers, added sugars, excess sodium, and highly engineered fats can help you make more informed choices. Rather than aiming for perfection, focus on gradually increasing the proportion of whole and minimally processed foods in your diet. Even modest dietary improvements can support heart health, metabolic health, and overall well-being over time. Sources World Health Organization (WHO): Healthy Diet Guidelines International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC): Processed Meat and Cancer Classification European Food Safety Authority (EFSA): Food Additives and Food Safety U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA): Food Additives and Ingredient Information Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health: The Nutrition Source British Heart Foundation: Healthy Eating Resources Disclaimer This article is intended for informational and educational purposes only and should not be considered medical advice. Nutrition needs vary by individual. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional or registered dietitian before making significant dietary changes or if you have concerns about your health or existing medical conditions.

title: Best online writing classes for kids: what to look for and where to start
summary: The best online writing classes give your kid real feedback on their actual writing from a live teacher who coaches revision. Here's what to look for, how the main options compare, what they cost, and how to match a class to your writer.
body_text: How much do online writing classes cost? Game-based apps like Night Zookeeper run about the price of a streaming subscription. Self-paced course platforms cost a bit more. Live classes cost the most, because you're paying for a trained teacher to read and respond to your kid's writing, and prices range widely between an ongoing group writing club, a short essay boot camp, and 1:1 coaching (usually the priciest but the most targeted, especially for a kid with a specific goal like a college essay or a struggling writer who needs one-on-one attention). Here's the honest part: you don't have to outsource all of writing. Many families teach the basics themselves and bring in one live class or a few 1:1 sessions for the part they can't coach, like giving objective feedback on a teenager's essay. It comes down to your budget and where you actually want the help. If your family has an education savings account (ESA), live online classes are an approved expense in many states, which can turn 1:1 writing coaching from out-of-pocket into funded. Our guide to ESA approved expenses walks through what qualifies. How to match a class to your writer Start with what your kid actually needs to work on, not their grade. The reluctant writer: a low-pressure creative writing club that builds enthusiasm before mechanics, paired with our guide on teaching writing to a child who refuses . The kid who loves stories: a creative writing class or club where they draft, share, and revise fiction with peers. The kid heading into essays: an academic or essay writing class that teaches structure and argument, backed by our grade-by-grade guide to teaching essay writing . The kid who needs a spark: if the block is ideas rather than skill, start with writing prompts by grade level and add a class once they're writing regularly. Questions parents ask Can I use online classes for all of my kid's writing instruction? Yes. Plenty of families run writing entirely through a live class or ongoing writing club, especially with a strong teacher and a consistent weekly rhythm. Whether that's the right call is a budget-and-preference question: it's most affordable with ESA funds, and it works best when you want an experienced teacher giving objective feedback rather than grading your own kid's writing yourself. My kid already writes a lot on their own. Do they need a class? Volume isn't the same as improvement. A kid can write pages and repeat the same habits every time. What moves a writer forward is targeted feedback and revision, and that's exactly what a class adds that solo writing can't. How do I know the teacher can actually teach writing? On a marketplace, check the teacher's profile for a writing or English-teaching background, a specific method they follow, and reviews from other parents. For writing especially, look for evidence they give real feedback, not just assign prompts. What age should kids start writing classes? Kids can start creative, story-based writing as early as ages 6 or 7, once they're reading and can get words on a page. Structured essay and academic writing usually starts around the upper elementary and middle school years. An older or struggling writer can start targeted instruction at any age, it's never too late to build the skill. The goal isn't the single "best" writing class. It's a class where a knowledgeable teacher reads your specific kid's writing and coaches the next revision. Start with what your writer needs to work on, look for real feedback and explicit instruction, and go from there. You can browse live online writing classes for kids on Outschool to see what's running now. Sources [1] Graham, S., & Perin, D. (2007). Writing Next: Effective strategies to improve writing of adolescents in middle and high schools . Carnegie Corporation of New York. carnegie.org (Writing Next report) [2] "Differentiation approach in education: Tailoring instruction for diverse learners," PMC (2025). pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11786651

title: 5 financial crime trends to watch in 2023
summary: This CGI blog discusses 5 financial crime trends to watch in 2023.
body_text: As financial crime continues to rise, keeping track of the trends in this volatile area is both important and challenging. To help you keep pace, this blog covers five of the top trends to watch in the coming months based on numerous financial crime outlooks that have been published in recent weeks. Although each trend is pressing, we prioritized them based on the level of effort we expect each to require, starting from the highest. 1. Enhancing the effectiveness of sanctions, both old and new New sanctions will continue to challenge existing compliance processes and demand innovative technology solutions. Last year, we saw the adoption of complex sanction schemes and a focus on sanctioning the widest possible spectrum of entities and individuals. The big focus this year will be, presumably and hopefully, on enhancing the effectiveness of these sanction schemes. For financial institutions, the rise in new sanctions has created the challenge of correctly identifying the type of countermeasure issued against an entity or a person in any given jurisdiction and how this affects a particular transaction at hand. Even more daunting perhaps is the need to understand complex beneficial ownership and related control structures, which can transfer risk to an entity not otherwise sanctioned. Beneficial ownership is a key part of effective sanctions implementation and requires data, globally unified definitions and thresholds, systems interconnectivity, and access to beneficial ownership registers. While there is ongoing concern about handling complex corporate structures, a large number of screening solutions still struggle with handling simple date-of-birth formats, name matching, and transliterations, even in the case of structured messages. As a result, many financial institutions will seek to enhance their screening capabilities, and many will resort to changing their solution providers. This is one of those big market moments, which has the potential to disrupt the usual incumbent solution providers. 2. Real-time everything, all at once Another key trend is the continued global rise in consumer demand for instant services—from onboarding, to purchasing financial products (e.g., insurance, mutual funds, loans), to domestic and international payments. This requires parallel developments in anti-financial crime (AFC) solutions. Know your customer (KYC) systems, sanctions and embargo screening engines, and anti-fraud programs are now expected to assess the risk of a potential customer or a transaction before any actions take place. In other words, AFC solutions must operate in real time or, at a minimum, predict outcomes with a reasonable degree of reliability, as well as learn from their mistakes. Add this “real-time everything” requirement to the unprecedented complexity of sanctions discussed above, and it makes for an interesting challenge for compliance teams and technology providers. Even more challenging is that many financial service providers (e.g., Revolut) facilitate instant money transfers across borders and currencies. For example, you can quickly transfer money to your friend who paid for your lunch. That, alone, is not an issue. The challenge comes when you consider screening messages a sender shares with a recipient. These messages can provide valuable insights into the purpose of potentially suspicious transactions. Further, they’re delivered in various formats, including GIF (animated picture). Which anti-money laundering (AML) program is ready to manage this degree of screening? Many financial regulators across European and North American markets are evaluating the levels of screening required for domestic and/or instant payments for exactly this reason. We recommend that banks and payment providers participate in industry consultations and working groups whenever possible to identify new ways for screening payments that are both effective and realistic. 3. The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) Related to the trends above are ever-expanding pools of complex data, which increase the demand for more resources. Extensive and expensive compliance teams can’t spend the majority of their time dealing with false positives. AI is a solution. As AI models improve the delivery of effective alert prioritization and regulators accept and become more comfortable with this process, banks will rush to implement AI layers on top of rules-based models to their existing systems, at least for the foreseeable future. Regulatory acceptance of proven AI models, however, is crucial. The mass adoption of AI will be rapid once regulators concede to the fact that dedicating more resources to higher-risk alerts requires that less attention and resources is dedicated to lower-risk alerts. In other words, something has to give, and AI can tell us what that should be. AI also will continue to expand its already meaningful footprint in customer onboarding, document validation, and fraud detection, especially in light of the continued real-time revolution. During a time of great economic uncertainty, fraud and other financial crime typically rises. We need to prepare not just for higher volumes, but also for new and unexpected ways in which criminals seek to defraud individuals and entities. AI can help with all of the above in two main ways. It can alert banks to new anomalies in customer behavior faster, including in areas such as social engineering fraud, which is often difficult to detect through traditional anti-fraud systems. It also can help manage large percentages of false positives, an industry-wide challenge, through effective prioritization. Institutions that are interested in exploring the potential of machine learning in this area should try to define their objectives as clearly as possible and conduct initial proof-of-concept pilots with an AI provider. Correct design of the data sample and research questions is crucial and will help banks make a business case for AI with their regulators. 4. Information sharing, greater cooperation, and joint actions Initiatives to advance data, information and knowledge sharing are gaining momentum quickly as we realize that our collective success rate in detecting organized crime and stopping illicit financial flows needs a big boost. During 2022, major international organizations and AFC standard-setters published reports and recommendations on how to implement such initiatives, as well as on how to navigate privacy concerns while allowing for greater transparency. One of their key recommendations is to clearly define specific use cases and deploy advanced privacy-enhancing technology through collaboration. Collaborative initiatives can range from thematic public-private partnerships, such as Canada’s Project Anton (an anti-wildlife trafficking initiative led by Scotiabank and FINTRAC), TMNL (a Dutch transaction monitoring consortium of five private banks), or the Singaporean COSMIC FI-FI (an information-sharing platform mandating financial institutions to alert others to suspicious behavior). However, this collaboration trend goes beyond just sharing. It also involves aligning interests, expectations, and legal and regulatory frameworks. This year, the European Union (EU) is operationalizing its planned Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA), which will consolidate regulatory approaches and oversee AML across the EU. This should make doing business across the EU smoother for banks, as well as their customers. Banks with operations across multiple EU states can start taking advantage of this by ensuring interoperability of their systems, data formats, and processes. 5. Increased focus on non-banking areas Policymakers and regulators increasingly are aware of how some professional services enable sanctioned or otherwise illicit assets to flow to and from our financial systems. These include legal advisory, accounting, real estate brokerage, or strategy consulting services. Professional services will continue to gain increased attention from policymakers, as well as supervisory bodies. A practical example are the sectoral sanctions imposed against the export of professional services to Russia last year. Gambling and gaming, in a similar vein, will receive plenty of attention from regulators in an effort to curb the flow of dirty money through related activities. A case in point is the UK’s Gambling Commission, which imposed a heavy fine in January 2023 for a gaming company’s “social responsibility and money laundering failings.” Increased attention to non-banking areas will be one of the main driving forces behind the growth of the AML outsourcing market, which is predicted to double in the next five years. AFC technology providers will need to develop risk and business models to cater to these customers. In addition, banks, asset managers, insurers, and others will want to evaluate their KYC/KYB and transaction monitoring systems to ensure they adequately monitor customers and activities with higher potential risks and align risk models with slight shifts in regulatory scrutiny. The bottom line is that our collective success in preventing, detecting, freezing and/or seizing illicit financial flows and fraudulent activities is fairly low, and something will have to give. We need to continue making progress at all levels—at the policy table, as part of regulatory enforcement, with technological advancement, and through greater collaboration. 1According to The State of Financial Crime 2023 Report, 99% of surveyed compliance respondents are planning to “re-evaluate their risk profile” this year, and more than a half are planning to hire and/or go through technological and organizational transformations. CGI has worked with financial institutions for the past four decades to build, implement and manage AFC solutions that not only prevent and reduce crime but also improve the bottom line. To learn more about our experience and capabilities, or to further discuss these trends, feel free to contact me . 1 “This report is based on a survey of 800 C-suite and senior compliance decision-makers across the U.S., Canada, UK, France, Germany, Netherlands, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Australia”. The ComplyAdvantage report can be downloaded here: https://complyadvantage.com/press-media/complyadvantage-releases-2022-state-of-financial-crime-report/ [Source information]

title: AI SDR vs human SDR: Which should you hire?
summary: An honest comparison of AI SDRs and human SDRs, where each wins, the real costs, and why the best answer is usually both.
body_text: Hire an AI SDR (sales development representative) for consistent, high-volume top-of-funnel work (sourcing, research, personalized outreach, first-line replies) and a human SDR for complex, relationship-led deals and live discovery. Most teams should not choose one; they should pair them, letting the AI remove the grunt work so human reps spend their time selling. The AI augments the team; it does not replace it. Here is the honest both-sides breakdown, including where a human clearly wins. AI SDR vs human SDR: The honest comparison Dimension AI SDR / AI BDR Human SDR / BDR Cost About one-fifth the pipeline cost, usage-based $120K-200K fully loaded/year Ramp time Effectively none 3-6 months Availability Continuous Working hours Volume Thousands of personalized sends Limited by hours in the day Personalization Per-lead at scale High quality, low volume Complex deals Weak; needs a human Strong Relationships and rapport Limited Core strength Live discovery calls Limited Strong Turnover risk None About 14-month average tenure Neither column wins outright. They are good at different things, which is why the framing "AI or human" usually leads to the wrong decision. Where does an AI SDR win? An AI SDR wins on the parts of the job that are volume, consistency, and speed, the parts that make human reps miserable and cost the most in wasted six-figure salary. Volume and coverage. It sources from a database of over 270M contacts, enriches and prioritizes, and runs personalized multichannel campaigns across far more accounts than a person can touch. Personalization at scale. Marketo-scale with a one-to-one feel: two people in the same campaign receive completely different messages, not a name-and-title swap. Consistency. No bad days, no ramp, no forgetting the follow-up. It replies to every inbound, qualifies, answers objections from a knowledge base, and chases follow-ups on schedule. Cost and scale economics. Roughly one-fifth the cost of a human BDR, usage-based, flat as the team grows. SumUp reported a $52 cost per lead; CookUnity about $45. Removing the busywork. SDRs spend 40-60% of hours on non-selling tasks and 66% of BDR time on outreach mechanics. That is exactly what the AI absorbs. See our full ranking of the best AI SDRs . Where does a human SDR win? This is the part vendors skip, so let's be direct. A human SDR wins wherever the deal depends on a person. Complex, high-consideration deals. Multi-stakeholder enterprise sales where the early relationship is the wedge. A human reads the room; the AI does not. Live discovery and objection handling. Real-time conversation, reading tone, improvising, and building trust on a call are human strengths. Creative and strategic judgment. Deciding which accounts to chase, reworking a broken message strategy, spotting a non-obvious angle. AI optimizes within a strategy; humans set it. Long-term relationships. Champions, referrals, and the trust that closes and renews deals live with people. If your motion is a handful of large, relationship-led deals a quarter, then a human SDR, or an account executive (AE), is the right hire, and an AI SDR is a support tool, not the driver. AI BDR vs human BDR: Is it any different? No. BDR (business development representative) and SDR describe the same function under different titles (BDR often skews to net-new outbound, SDR to inbound qualification, but the split varies by company), and the AI-vs-human tradeoffs are identical. An AI BDR excels at net-new sourcing and personalized outbound at volume; a human BDR excels at the deals and conversations that need a person. The decision framework below applies to both terms. For the equivalent field on the BDR side, see the best AI BDRs . Should you hire an AI SDR or a human SDR? A decision framework Ask three questions: 1. What is your deal shape? High-volume, transactional, or product-led? Lean AI-first. Large, complex, relationship-led? Keep humans central and use AI for support. 2. Where is your team's time going? If reps spend 40-60% of their time on list building, research, and sending, you are paying six figures for busywork. Hand that to AI and redeploy the humans to selling. 3. What are you scaling? Need 3x the top-of-funnel volume? Adding three human BDRs costs $360K-600K plus ramp and turnover. An AI BDR scales volume without the seat multiplier. For most teams the answer is both, sequenced right: the AI owns sourcing, outreach, and first-line replies; humans own qualified conversations and closing. That is augmentation, and it is why over 90% of Artisan customers run the AI autonomously for the top of the funnel while their reps focus downstream. Ava removes the grunt work so reps sell; she does not replace the team. What does the augmented model look like in practice? At larger organizations the pattern is central deployment: sales ops runs the AI BDR for an entire AE team who never log in, and every qualified meeting routes to the right rep by CRM ownership. The reps never build a list or send a cold email; they walk into booked conversations. SaaStr's Jason Lemkin, after scaling outreach with Ava, said "the AI emails are actually better than what our humans produced. Consistently better," which is the tell: the AI is a better top-of-funnel engine that frees people for the work only people can do. Teams weighing the broader go-to-market (GTM) stack can compare the best AI GTM platforms and the 15 best AI sales tools . FAQ AI SDR vs human SDR: Which is better? Neither is universally better; they are better at different things. An AI SDR wins on volume, personalization at scale, consistency, and cost (roughly one-fifth of a human's). A human SDR wins on complex deals, live discovery, rapport, and strategy. For most teams the strongest setup pairs them: AI owns top-of-funnel, humans own relationships and closing. AI BDR vs human BDR: Which is better? Same answer as AI vs human SDR, since BDR and SDR describe the same job. An AI BDR is better for high-volume net-new sourcing and personalized outbound; a human BDR is better for relationship-led, multi-stakeholder deals. The best result usually comes from augmentation: the AI handles the mechanical 40-60% of the work, and people handle the conversations that need judgment. Should I replace my SDRs with AI? Usually not outright. The stronger move is to remove the busywork (list building, research, sending, first-line replies) with AI so your reps spend their time selling and closing. AI amplifies a good team; it does not substitute for human judgment on complex deals. Replacing wholesale only makes sense for purely transactional, high-volume motions, and even then humans typically handle qualified conversations. Is an AI SDR cheaper than a human SDR? Yes, for top-of-funnel work. A human SDR costs $120K-200K fully loaded per year with a 3-6 month ramp and about 14-month average tenure. An AI SDR generates pipeline at about one-fifth the cost, usage-based, with no ramp or turnover. But cost is only decisive where the work is volume-driven; for relationship-led deals the human's higher cost buys something the AI cannot. Can an AI SDR and human SDR work together? Yes, and that is the recommended model. The AI sources, enriches, personalizes, sends, and handles first-line replies, then books qualified meetings onto reps' calendars by CRM ownership. Humans take those conversations, run discovery, handle complex objections, and close. The AI removes the 40-60% of time reps waste on busywork so they focus on selling. What can a human SDR do that an AI SDR cannot? Read a room on a live call, build genuine rapport and long-term relationships, improvise through complex multi-stakeholder deals, and set strategy (which accounts to pursue, when to change the approach). AI executes and optimizes within a defined strategy and excels at volume and consistency, but the creative and relational judgment that closes big deals remains human. The takeaway AI SDR vs human SDR is the wrong question for most teams. The right one is how to combine them: let the AI own the high-volume, low-judgment top of the funnel, and let your people own the relationships and deals that need a human.
